Data analysis

Translating : This translation was done using an AI tool.

Contexte

Facing growing demand and fierce competition, a major retail chain is seeking your expertise to identify the most effective strategies. It wants to determine which products, regions, categories, and customer segments to target or avoid.
Feel free to let your imagination run wild with the data, but also make sure to provide relevant business insights to help improve them.

Between 2014 and the end of 2017, this company generated cumulative revenue of $2,295,274. During this period, it posted a profit of $285,988.30, representing a margin of 12.46% of total revenue.

Graphical representation by year

df |> 
  group_by(order_year) |>
  summarise(montant_total_annee = sum(Sales)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x=as.factor(order_year), y=montant_total_annee, fill=as.factor(order_year))) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = comma(montant_total_annee)),
    vjust = -0.5,
    size = 4
  ) + labs(
    x = "Années",
    y = "Chiffre d'affaire",
    title = "Chiffre d'affaire par an"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = .5)
  )

Revenue rose from $483,722 in 2014 to $732,515 in 2017, reflecting strong growth during this period. Examining this graph allows us to distinguish two phases of this growth:

  • 2014 - 2015 : During this period, the company’s revenue growth remained relatively stable, with a slight decline in 2015, falling from $483,722 to $470,533.

  • 2016 - 2017 : We observe a surge in the company’s revenue, rising from $470,533 to $608,505 in 2016, with this growth continuing into 2017 to reach $732,515.

Representation of turnover as a function of profit for :

  • Catégorie
df |> ggplot(aes(y = reorder(`Sub-Category`, Sales))) +
  geom_col(aes(x = Sales), fill = "grey75", width = 0.75) +
  geom_col(aes(x = marge), fill = "#2166AC", width = 0.35) +
  labs(
    title = "Ventes totales et marge par sous-catégorie",
    x = "Montant ($)",
    y = "Sous-catégorie"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )

The chart above compares total sales (gray bars) and margins generated (blue bars) for each sub-category. We can derive several key insights from this:

  • In terms of total sales : Chairs and Phones clearly dominate sales, making them the company’s primary sales drivers (with revenue exceeding $300,000). The Storage, Tables, and Binders sub-categories show significant sales volume, exceeding $200,000.

  • In terms of profitability, the “Papers” sub-category stands out as the highest margin generator, despite having total sales figures well below those of “Chairs” and “Phones.” “Furnishings,” “Envelopes,” and “Art” also yield significant margins, making them key contributors to the company’s bottom line. The “Labels” sub-category appears anomalous, as it generates a profit margin exceeding 100% of revenue—a result that is logically abnormal.

  • Conversely, several sub-categories show negative profit margins despite varying sales volumes. This is particularly true for Binders, Appliances, and Tables, which post negative profits, indicating business segments that generate significant revenue losses for the company. Other sub-categories, such as Copiers, Machines, Bookcases, and Fasteners, show margins that are virtually zero or relatively modest.

Study of the impact of discounts on margins

df |> ggplot(aes(x = Discount, y = marge)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "black") +
  labs(
    title = "Marge en fonction du discount",
    x = "Discount",
    y = "Marge"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
cor.test(df$marge, df$Discount, method = "spearman")
Warning in cor.test.default(df$marge, df$Discount, method = "spearman"): Cannot
compute exact p-value with ties

    Spearman's rank correlation rho

data:  df$marge and df$Discount
S = 2.7319e+11, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
sample estimates:
       rho 
-0.6450828

Shown above are the profit margins realized by the company based on the discount granted. We immediately observe a negative relationship: as the discount increases, the margin collapses—a trend that becomes critical once the company reaches the 50% discount threshold.

A Spearman correlation coefficient of -0.6450828 confirms our visual assessment: margin and discount are negatively correlated.

Je choisis comme référence, celle dont l’entreprise a réalisé le plus de chiffre d’affaire:

  • Phones pour les sous-catégories,

  • West pour la région

For the shipping method, I am selecting the default option: Standard Class.

tableau_regression <- df |> mutate(
  discount_categorielle = cut(
    df$Discount, 
    breaks = c(-Inf, 0, 0.2, 0.5, Inf), 
    labels = c("Pas de remise", "1% à 20 %", "21% à 50 %", "Sup. à 50 %")
  ),
  sub_category = as_factor(`Sub-Category`),
  ship_mode = `Ship Mode`,
  sub_category = fct_relevel(sub_category, "Phones", after = 0),
  Region = fct_relevel(Region, "West", after = 0),
  ship_mode = fct_relevel(ship_mode, "Standard Class", after = 0)
)
regression <- lm(marge ~ discount_categorielle * sub_category + Region  + ship_mode + Segment, data = tableau_regression)
tbl_regression(regression)

Abréviation: IC = intervalle de confiance

The dependent variable is the profit margin realized by the company, and the beta column represents the average effect—ceteris paribus—relative to the reference category denoted as “—”. Here are some interpretations of the factors that have a statistically significant effect on the margin:

  • Discount : The intuition noted earlier is borne out by our regression model: each reduction step significantly erodes the profit margin.

    • A discount of 1% to 20% reduces the profit margin by an average of 16 percentage points compared to the “no discount” baseline.

    • A reduction of 21% to 50% lowers the margin by an average of 48 percentage points.

    • And a discount of more than 50% causes the company to lose money, with an average margin that is 146 percentage points lower.

  • The region has a more mixed influence on the margin: The sale in the Central region has a significant importance on the margin, it reduces it by 6.6 percentage points compared to the sale in the West region. The South and East regions, on the other hand, have a limited incidence which are respectively 1.6 and 1.9 percentage points less.

  • The impact of sub-categories on margins varies significantly depending on the level of discount granted :

  • Certain subgroups show a marked positive effect at high discount levels, despite a null or negative effect at lower levels :

    • Furnishings: no significant effect at 1–20% (-1.5, p=0.3), followed by a massive effect of +51 (>50% discount, p<0.001)

    • Copiers: no significant effect at 1–20% (+2.2, p=0.6), then +14 (20–50% discount, p=0.023)

    • Chairs: significant negative effect at 1–20% (-4.4, p=0.016), shifting to +15 (20–50% discount, p<0.001)

  • A significant positive effect only at low discount levels (1% to 20%): Fasteners (+5.8, p=0.011), Envelopes (+5.2, p=0.015), Paper (+5.0, p<0.001), Labels (+4.2, p=0.029).

  • One group shows a significant negative effect starting at the low discount level, which persists for subcategories where data is available at the next tier. :

    • Tables: -5.0 (1–20%, borderline significance, p=0.060), then -6.8 (20–50%, p=0.009)

    • Storage: -4.0 (1–20%, p=0.008); data missing at higher levels.

    • Supplies: -6.3 (1–20%, p=0.010); data missing at higher levels.

  • Three categories stand out due to a catastrophic effect at high discount levels, with no significant effect at lower levels :

    • Appliances: no significant effect at 1–20% (-0.57, p=0.8), followed by the sharpest drop in the table, to -130 (>50%, p<0.001).

    • Bookcases: no significant effect at 1–20% (-2.9, p=0.3) or 20–50% (+0.95, p=0.8), followed by a sharp shift to -40 (>50%, p<0.001).

    • Binders: no significant effect at 1–20% (+1.1, p=0.5), then -9.2 (>50%, p=0.027)

  • Categories with no significant effect detected at any level: Art (+1.1, p=0.5), Accessories (-0.33, p=0.8), Machines (-3.3 then +1.8, p=0.4 and p=0.7).

  • Conversely, ship mode and segment have no statistically significant impact on the company’s margin.

Trends in sales and margins over time

serie_mensuelle <- tableau_regression %>%
  mutate(mois = floor_date(as.Date(order_date), unit = "month")) %>%
  group_by(mois) %>%
  summarise(
    sales_total = sum(Sales, na.rm = TRUE),
    profit_total = sum(Profit, na.rm = TRUE),
    marge_moyenne = mean(marge, na.rm = TRUE),
    n_commandes = n()
  ) %>%
  arrange(mois)
ts_sales <- ts(serie_mensuelle$sales_total, 
               start = c(year(min(serie_mensuelle$mois)), month(min(serie_mensuelle$mois))), 
               frequency = 12)
decomp <- decompose(ts_sales, type = "multiplicative")
plot(decomp)
df_prophet <- serie_mensuelle %>%
  rename(ds = mois, y = sales_total)
modele_prophet <- prophet(df_prophet)

This model forecasts sales trends beyond 2017, assuming no changes to our strategy. :

  • Real growth: the sales trajectory has been structurally upward since 2014. The brand is not in decline, but this growth follows a very distinct pattern, with the bulk of activity concentrated at the end of the year and a marked slowdown at the beginning.

  • The blue band that widens over time reflects a genuine business risk: the further we look ahead, the less we can blindly rely on a simple extrapolation of the past. In a fiercely competitive environment, this means that future sales will increasingly depend on strategic decisions made today rather than on a simple continuation of the past.

  • The demand is there and will continue to grow unless there is a drastic change—but the real battle is no longer about sales volume; it is about the ability to generate that growth without sacrificing margins, by managing discounting more precisely across categories and regions.
